---
title: "Method"
subtitle: "Features, an ablation, and an alert rule chosen without looking at the answer"
---

The model here is ordinary — a scikit-learn Isolation Forest, which is the most common
choice made on this dataset. What the project rests on is not the model but the layer
after it: a lead-time metric built so that it cannot be tuned into a flattering number,
and a comparison that tests the project's own central claim rather than assuming it.

**That comparison came out negative, and it is stated here rather than buried.** The
defect-frequency machinery works — it identifies which surface failed, on real data, in
three of four documented cases. It does not improve how early the failure is detected.
Both halves are below.

## Why a bearing defect has a frequency

A rolling-element bearing is a machine with known geometry, so a defect in it does not
produce generic "vibration". Each rolling element strikes the defect once per pass,
and the pass rate follows from the geometry and shaft speed alone. Four rates matter,
one per defect location:

| Frequency | Struck by | Indicates |
|---|---|---|
| BPFO — ball pass frequency, outer race | each ball passing a fixed outer-race point | outer-race spall |
| BPFI — ball pass frequency, inner race | each ball passing a point on the rotating inner race | inner-race spall |
| BSF — ball spin frequency | a defect on a ball itself, once per rotation | rolling-element defect |
| FTF — fundamental train frequency | the cage rotating | cage damage |

**[The data documentation](data.qmd) carries the numbers**: rig geometry, the four
frequencies it yields for this bearing, their provenance, and which one carries the signal
in which test. They are properties of the rig rather than choices made here, so they live
with the data and are stated once.

## What the detector reads

`loading.py` reduces each 20,480-sample acquisition to six statistics per channel: RMS,
mean, standard deviation, absolute maximum, excess kurtosis and skewness. `features.py`
then adds, for the RMS and kurtosis columns only, rolling mean, standard deviation and
maximum over windows of 10 and 50 files, plus first differences and their absolute values.

The published detector selects from that table by substring — `_rms`, `_kurt`, `_std`,
`_max` — and by the failed bearing's prefix. Mean and skewness are computed and then not
selected. For Test 3, Bearing 3 that is **20 columns**; for Test 1, which carries two
accelerometers per bearing, **40**.

- **RMS** — total vibration energy. The primary degradation indicator, and on this data it
  rises 11.4× above baseline before Test 3's bearing fails.
- **Kurtosis** — the fourth moment, sensitive to *impulsiveness* rather than amplitude. A
  spall produces sharp repeated impacts, which raise kurtosis while RMS is still near
  baseline, so it can lead RMS. Note this project computes **excess** kurtosis, where
  Gaussian reads 0 and not 3 — every threshold in the bearing literature is quoted 3 too
  high for this column. See [the data documentation](data.qmd).
- **Standard deviation and absolute maximum** — for a near-zero-mean signal the first is
  numerically close to RMS, and the second is the peak a crest factor would be built from.
- **The rolling and difference columns are 16 of the 20.** They carry the *rate* of
  degradation rather than its level, which is what lets an alert fire while the level
  itself is still unremarkable.

Every one of these is a time-domain quantity. None of them knows what a bearing is.

## The defect-frequency features

A second pass over the raw archive computes these per acquisition and writes them to
`data/processed/test{N}_spectral.csv`, which is committed — so everything below
reproduces from a clean clone without the 6.2 GB download.

**Frequency domain**, from a Welch power spectral density (PSD) estimate:

- **Defect-frequency band energy** — power in bands around BPFO, BPFI and BSF and their
  first three harmonics.
- **Spectral entropy** — how evenly energy is spread across the spectrum.
- **High-frequency ratio** — proportion of energy above 5 kHz.

**Envelope domain** — the same three bands, measured a different way, and it is the
physically correct way. A localised defect does not radiate at its defect frequency. Each
impact rings a structural resonance in the kHz range, so the defect rate appears as the
*modulation* of that resonance and carries no line of its own in the raw spectrum.
Band-passing to 2 kHz–Nyquist and taking the analytic-signal magnitude moves that
modulation to baseband, where it is a line again. This is standard practice for
rolling-element bearings, after Randall and Antoni (2011).

Two choices in there are worth stating because they were made against a rule rather than
by taste:

**Band width is derived, not picked.** The Welch estimate uses a 0.1 s window, giving
10 Hz bins, and a band must span at least three bins to be an integral rather than a point
sample. Before that rule, a fixed 5 Hz half-width resolved to exactly **one** bin at every
harmonic of every defect frequency, which made the width parameter inert.

**FTF gets no column, and the exclusion is derived too.** At 14.775 Hz no three-bin band
around it clears DC, where the bin carries the signal mean rather than defect energy. A
longer window would let it back in automatically. No test in this dataset has a cage
failure, which is what FTF diagnoses.

## The bands name the right fault

Fold change from a healthy window to the last 30 live acquisitions, on the envelope
spectrum, per bearing. Produced by notebook 02; the post-shutdown tail is measured per
run rather than assumed.

| Test | Documented failure | Dominant band on that bearing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bearing 3, **inner race** | BPFI **18.8×**, against BSF 17.4 and BPFO 10.3 | correct |
| 1 | Bearing 4, **roller element** | BPFO 15.0×, against BPFI 8.8 and BSF 8.4 | **missed** |
| 2 | Bearing 1, **outer race** | BPFO **150.1×**, against BPFI 10.4 and BSF 8.9 | correct |
| 3 | Bearing 3, **outer race** | BPFO **354.4×**, against BSF 42.1 and BPFI 38.5 | correct |

The failed bearing is also the loudest bearing on its shaft each time — 354× against 8.8×
for a healthy bearing in Test 3. So this is specificity, not merely sensitivity: it says
*which* surface on *which* bearing, which overall vibration amplitude cannot.

Three of four is the honest count. Bearing 4's roller-element defect in Test 1 is read as
outer race. Rolling-element and cage faults are the known-hard cases, and a roller defect
often shows at twice BSF rather than at BSF; this analysis looks only at the first three
harmonics of BSF itself.

This is a descriptive contrast between two windows, not a validated classifier. It uses
one hand-chosen healthy window and no held-out validation.

## They do not improve lead time

Five feature sets, scored with the selection procedure held identical throughout — same
contamination, same target false-alarm rate, the same fixed (k, m) candidate list and
first-that-passes rule, the same three-way healthy-window split, the same seed. Only the
scored columns differ.

| Feature set | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **published** — time domain, 20 columns | **79.5 h** | **53.7 h** | **57.0 h** |
| the same, log-scaled | 79.5 h | 53.8 h | 55.0 h |
| + PSD bands, entropy, high-frequency ratio | 79.5 h | 54.3 h | 50.7 h |
| + those, with rolling and difference columns | 10.5 h | 46.7 h | 57.8 h |
| + envelope bands | 79.7 h | 53.7 h | **58.5 h** |

Zero held-out false alarms in every one of the fifteen runs, in 323 / 147 / 949 files.

**The best spectral arm buys 0.2 h, 0.0 h and 1.5 h.** Acquisitions are ten minutes apart,
so Test 1's "gain" is one file.

**The reason is visible in where the alarm fires.** On Test 1 four of the five arms fire at
file 1829 or 1830 out of 2,156 — despite genuinely different models, with thresholds of
−0.153, −0.139, −0.178 and −0.136, and one arm selecting a 4-of-5 rule where the others
take 3-of-5. Different features, different detectors, the same moment. By the time
degradation crosses a threshold calibrated against healthy data, every feature has already
moved together; what is scored barely matters.

**More features made it worse, not better.** The arm with rolling and difference columns on
the spectral block carries 368 columns and is the worst on Test 1 by 303 files while being
second-best on Test 3. A feature set that swings that far between runs of the same rig is
not one that helps unevenly; it is one whose behaviour is not predictable from the others.

**The log-scaled arm is why any of this is attributable.** Spectral band energies span three
orders of magnitude and are strongly log-normal, so they have to be log-scaled to be usable
at all. Without an arm that applies the same transform to the time-domain features and
nothing else, the envelope arm's 1.5 h on Test 3 could have been credited to the physics —
when the change of scale alone accounts for −2.0 h on the same run.

## Three feature directions that are the opposite of the intuition

Each is a trap that produces a confidently wrong reading, so they are worth stating
plainly, together with how firmly each is established.

- **Spectral entropy is *higher* in healthy bearings, not lower.** The intuition says a
  fault means disorder means high entropy. The opposite holds: healthy bearing noise is
  broadband and close to flat, which is maximum entropy. A developing defect *concentrates*
  energy into BPFO harmonics — structure, not noise — and structure lowers entropy. Pinned
  by a test (`test_spectral_entropy_faulty_lower_than_healthy`) on synthetic signals, and
  it holds on all three runs in real data — 0.916 → 0.911, 0.850 → 0.774 and 0.911 → 0.860
  from a healthy window to the end. The direction is consistent; the magnitude is not, and
  on Test 1 it is barely a movement at all.
- **`high_freq_ratio` is documented to run the other way too**, on the reasoning that
  healthy Gaussian noise is already rich in high frequencies so a fault has little headroom
  to add any. **Measured, it does not hold universally.** It falls on the two outer-race
  runs — 0.128 → 0.122 and 0.318 → 0.232 — and *rises* on Test 1, 0.504 → 0.507. Test 1 is
  the inner-race failure, and an inner-race defect is amplitude-modulated by shaft rotation,
  which spreads energy into sidebands rather than concentrating it; that would explain the
  difference, but this project has not tested that explanation and it should be read as a
  hypothesis. Only the `[0, 1]` range is asserted by a test. **Do not rely on this feature's
  direction.**
- **`crest_factor` becomes unreliable at high fault severity.** It rises early, as discrete
  impacts appear against a quiet floor, then falls back once the defect is severe enough
  that impacts merge into a noise floor the fault itself has lifted. Read monotonically, it
  will eventually suggest the bearing is recovering. Only `crest_factor >= 1` is asserted by
  a test; the non-monotonicity is a documented caution here, and this dataset's runs end
  before it appears — crest factor is still rising at failure.

## The detector

`StandardScaler` → `PCA` (10 components) → `IsolationForest`, fitted on the **first 60%**
of each series on the assumption that a run-to-failure rig starts healthy, then scoring
the whole series. Isolation Forest suits the problem because it needs no labels and
isolates outliers by random partitioning, which is cheap and explainable.

An autoencoder path exists (PyTorch, optional install) and is handled correctly by the
metric layer, including its inverted sign convention. No autoencoder result is
published: it did not earn a place over the Isolation Forest on this data.

## Turning scores into an alert, without cheating

This is the part that took the work. Three problems have to be solved in order, and
each one is a precondition for the next.

### 1. `is_anomaly` cannot be used at all

`contamination=c` guarantees that fraction of the **training** window is labelled
anomalous, and the training window is the part assumed healthy. Measured: 5.03%, 5.08%
and 8.01% of training files flagged, against configured 0.05, 0.05 and 0.08. So the
label is doing what it was asked to do, and the first flagged file lands at or near
file 0 on every run. The lead time is therefore read from a **score threshold**, never
from `is_anomaly`.

### 2. A single flagged window is not an alert

Runs of consecutive flags occur by chance at those rates — a 10-of-10 rule still fires
at file 9 of Tests 2 and 3. The rule is **k of the last m** files flagged.

### 3. Choosing k and m is where a result gets fabricated

Picking the (k, m) that yields the nicest lead time is precisely the failure the
sustained rule exists to prevent, and it would be invisible in the output. Two things
prevent it here:

**The candidate list is fixed in advance**, ordered by window length then strictness —
3-of-5, 4-of-5, 5-of-5, 6-of-10, … 30-of-30 — and **the first entry that does not fire
on healthy data wins**. That is the *most sensitive* rule meeting the constraint, not
the best-scoring one. Lead time is never consulted during selection.

**The healthy region is split into three disjoint windows**, so no window both sets a
parameter and scores it:

| Window | Slice of the live series | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Calibration | first 10% | sets the score threshold, at a 1% per-file false-alarm rate |
| Selection | 10% – 25% | chooses k and m |
| Held out | 25% – 40% | reports the false-alarm rate — **never touched before this** |

The reported "0 false alarms in 323 / 147 / 949 files" comes from the third window
only, which is what makes it out-of-sample.

The 40% boundary is itself an assumption — a run that degraded early would push the
"healthy" window into the failure and report a real detection as a false positive — so
it is **checked rather than assumed**: `check_healthy_region` verifies RMS stays below
2× baseline throughout. All three runs pass.

### 4. The post-shutdown tail

Each rig auto-terminates on a debris-triggered switch, and the acquisitions after that
read near-zero RMS on every channel. They are not healthy readings, and they must not
anchor a lead time. The tail is **measured per run, not assumed** — 0 files for Test 1,
2 for Test 2, 1 for Test 3 — by requiring *every* bearing to fall below 0.2× baseline,
because one bearing can go quiet through damage but all four go quiet only when the
shaft stops. Test 1 never went quiet at all and ends on its RMS peak, so the usual
"drop the last file" would have discarded the very failure being measured. Details in
[the data documentation](data.qmd).

## What this does not establish

- **The ablation is one dataset and three runs.** That the defect-frequency features add
  nothing here is not a claim that they add nothing. This rig is heavily loaded and runs to
  destruction, so degradation is large and monotone by the time it is detectable at all —
  the regime that most favours a plain amplitude feature. A lightly loaded machine, or one
  where the question is *which* surface is failing rather than *whether* one is, is exactly
  where the band features would be expected to pay.
- **A negative ablation is not a licence to delete the features.** They answer a different
  question, and they answer it correctly: three of four documented failure modes, named
  from vibration alone.
- **Three runs is three samples.** The alert rule is selected per run against that
  run's own healthy data. That is correct procedure, and it is not the same as
  validating a fixed rule on an unseen rig.
- **Zero false alarms is an upper bound.** 147 to 949 held-out files cannot resolve a
  rate below roughly 1 in 1,000.
- **Lead time is anchored on the end of the run.** The rigs ran to destruction, so the
  last live acquisition is taken as the failure — but no independent ground-truth
  failure timestamp exists to check that against, and it ties the number to when the
  rig happened to stop.
